SA.1 value: Participants generally preferred in-person counselling or saw the chatbot as a supplement rather than replacement. Services for LGBTQI communities are concentrated in urban centres, making access difficult for those in outlying areas. Most participants reported access to only 'a little or some' psychosocial support.
SA.2 value: Participants valued privacy and anonymity as major benefits, with stigma and judgment being key concerns. Stigma (anti-MSM stigma, internalised stigma, concealment of sexual identity) drives mental health distress and prevents engagement with services. Fear of stigma and judgment often prevent engagement with mental and other health services among key populations.
SA.3 value: Interviews conducted in English or isiZulu. Multilingual capabilities deemed essential, with participants requesting isiZulu and isiXhosa support. Code-switching difficulties noted when expressing emotions in English vs local languages.
SA.5 value: Mental health support services remain poorly accessible to most people. There is a severe shortage of mental health providers in South Africa and other low- and middle-income countries. Limited options available for LGBTQI+ community members to access services focused on their health needs, and where available, they are concentrated in urban centres, making access difficult for those in outlying areas.
SA.8 value: No specific reading age or literacy level estimates provided. However, voice-based interactions were recommended to make the chatbot accessible to low-literate users or those who cannot read English.
